title: Thoreau's sauntering
hookLine: in his essay Walking (1862), Thoreau praises going out with no destination

cards: When did you last go out with no errand? Not to the store, not to hit a step count, not walking the dog on its schedule. Just out the door, turning left because left looked nice.

If the answer takes a while to find, that's an answer too. A man in Concord, Massachusetts, spent hours a day doing exactly that, and treated it as serious work. He wrote an essay about it, printed in the year he died.

teach.b: Henry David Thoreau wrote Walden, about his life in a cabin by a pond. But his essay Walking, published in the Atlantic in 1862, just after his death, has a lighter step.
It opens boldly: "I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness."
He says he's met only one or two people in his life who understood the art of walking, people "who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering." Then he plays with where the word saunter comes from.
One story, he says, is that it comes from wanderers in the Middle Ages who asked for charity on their way, they claimed, to the Holy Land, la Sainte Terre.
So a saunterer is a Holy-Lander, and every walk can be a small pilgrimage. Another story he offers: sans terre, without land or home, and so at home everywhere.
The honest part: modern dictionaries say nobody really knows where saunter comes from, and Thoreau's stories read more like poetry than history. But look at what he's doing with them.
A walk without a destination isn't lazy. It's a kind of pilgrimage, where the holy land is wherever your feet happen to be.
He claimed he needed four hours a day of it to stay well in body and spirit. You don't need four hours. You need one walk where nothing is the goal.

how: Some readers of Thoreau take aimless walks in his spirit, without a route or a goal, and his essay Walking is still read by hikers and nature writers.

games.q: you're Thoreau at your door in Concord. where are you going?
o: the same loop as always, timed.
games.why: nowhere in particular. for Thoreau, a walk without a destination was a small pilgrimage, and the holy land was wherever he stood.

practice: Picture your front door, then picture stepping out and turning whichever way looks inviting: no errand, no route, no timer except a rough sense of when to head home.
Notice what that feels like in your body, freedom or a little itch to be useful. Both are fine.
